title: Bishops from Paul's Roman letter, continued
english: became bishop of Macedonia. 20. Stachys, whom Paul also mentions in the same letter, was appointed first bishop of Byzantium by the apostle Andrew in Argyropolis of Thrace. 21. Apelles, whom Paul also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of Smyrna before Saint Polycarp. 22. Aristobulus, whom Paul also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of Britain. 23. Narcissus, whom the same apostle also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of Athens. 24. Herodion, whom the same apostle also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of Patras. 25. Rufus, whom the same apostle also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of Thebes. 26. Asyncritus, whom the same apostle also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of Hyrcania. 27. Phlegon, whom the same apostle also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of Marathon. 28. Hermes, whom the same apostle also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of Dalmatia. 29. Hermas, whom the same apostle also mentions in the same letter, became bishop of the city of Philippi. 30. Patrobas, whom the same apostle Paul also mentions, became bishop in Ne Potiolis. 31. Agabus, who is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, was also deemed worthy of the prophetic gift. 32. Linus, whom the apostle Paul also mentions, became the first bishop of Rome after Peter the chief. 33. Gaius, whom the apostle Paul also mentions, became bishop of Ephesus after Timothy. 34. Philologus, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Sinope, appointed by Andrew. 35. Olympas, whom Paul also mentions, was martyred in Rome together with Peter the chief, having his head cut off. 36. Rhodion, whom Paul also mentions, was likewise perfected by martyrdom in Rome with Peter and Olympas, he too having his head cut off. 38. Jason, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Tarsus. 39. Sosipater, whom Paul likewise also mentions, became bishop of Iconium. 40. Lucius, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop in Laodicea of Syria. 41.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Epiphanius continues his numbered catalogue of the seventy disciples, listing those Paul mentions in the letter to the Romans and where each became bishop.

title: Later disciples as bishops with heresy and desertion noted
english: 41. Tertius, who wrote Paul's letter to the Romans, became the second bishop of Iconium. 42. Erastus, whom Paul also mentions in the same letter, became steward of the church in Jerusalem, and afterward became bishop of Paneas. 43. Phygelus, whom Paul also mentions as having fallen into heresy and shared Simon's views, became bishop of Ephesus. 44. Hermogenes, whom Paul likewise mentions as having fallen into heresy, became bishop in Megara.

45. Demas, whom the apostle Paul likewise mentions as having apostatized, abandoned the faith. For in his second letter to Timothy Paul speaks about all three: Phygelus and Hermogenes fell into heresy and opposed his teaching, but Demas loved this present world and abandoned the gospel message (2 Timothy 4:10), and became a priest of idols in Thessalonica. About such people John the apostle also wrote, "They went out from us, but they did not belong to us" (1 John 2:19).

46. Quartus, whom Paul also mentions in his letter to the Romans, became bishop of Beirut. 47. Apollos, whom Paul also mentions in his letter to the Corinthians, became bishop of Caesarea. 48. Cephas, whom the apostle Paul rebuked in Antioch and who shares his name with Peter, became bishop of Conia. 49. Sosthenes, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Colophonias. 50. Epaphroditus, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Adriake. 51. Caesar, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Dyrrachium. 52. Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Apollonias. 53. Joseph, also called Justus and Barsabbas, whom Luke mentions in the Acts of the Apostles as the one put to the lot alongside Matthias, became bishop of Eleutheropolis.

54. Artemas, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop in Lystra. 55. Clement, whom Paul also mentions when he says, "with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers" (Philippians 4:3), became bishop of Sardica. He was the first from the Gentiles and the Greeks to believe in Christ. 56. Onesiphorus, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Coronea. 57. Tychicus, whom Paul also mentions, became the first bishop of Chalcedon in Bithynia. 58. Carpus, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Beroea in Thrace.
added_allusions: Reference to 2 Timothy 2:20-21 regarding Phygellus and Hermogenes
Reference to 1 John 2:19 regarding those who departed from the faith
Reference to Acts 1:23-26 regarding the selection of Matthias
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Epiphanius continues his catalogue of the seventy disciples, naming the city where each served as bishop.

title: End of the seventy and names of the twelve
english: 59. Euodus, whom Paul also mentions, became the first bishop of Antioch after Peter the chief. 60. Philemon, to whom Paul wrote a personal letter, became bishop of Gaza. 61. Zenas the lawyer, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Diospolis. 62. Aquila, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Heraclea. 63. Priscas, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Colophon. 64. Junias, whom Paul also mentions, became bishop of Apamea in Syria.

65. Mark, also called John, whom Luke mentions in the Acts of the Apostles, became bishop of Byblos. 66. Aristarchus, whom Paul also mentions. 67. Pudens, whom Paul also mentions. 68. Trophimus, whom the apostle Paul also mentions. These three shared all the persecutions of the apostle Paul and suffered with him, and in the end they were perfected with him through martyrdom under Nero, beheaded with him. With Mark and Luke the evangelist counted with them, they come to seventy together.
By Saint Epiphanius, Archbishop of Cyprus. These are the names of the twelve apostles.

1. Peter, who was also called Simon and Cephas and Symeon. 2. Andrew, his brother. 3. James. 4. John. These two were called Boanerges, which is interpreted sons of thunder. 5. Philip. 6. Bartholomew. 7. Matthew the tax collector. 8. Thomas, who was also called Didymus. 9. James son of Alphaeus. 10. Thaddaeus. Matthew calls him Lebbaeus, Luke calls him Judas son of James, and Mark calls him Levi sitting at the tax office. 11. Simon the Cananaean. 12. Judas Iscariot, and Matthias entered in his place.

Peter and Andrew were brothers, the sons of Annas. James and John were the sons of Zebedee. James and Judas were the sons of Alphaeus. The fishermen were Peter and Andrew, James and John. As for James, who is called brother of the Lord, which one was it who became bishop of Jerusalem, called the Just. One James was the son of Zebedee and the other was the son of Alphaeus, and the other was the son of Joseph the betrothed, as the Jews said. Matthew says that Simon and Judas and Joseph the brother were called tax collectors, and Luke says that Levi too was called a tax collector. Jonah is interpreted dove.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Epiphanius finishes listing the seventy disciples and then gives the list of the twelve apostles with notes on their families.
